Logistic regression with SPSS-style output

Source: R/models.R
jlogistic.Rd

Fits a binary logistic regression using stats::glm() with family = binomial and prints formatted output including an omnibus model test, model summary statistics, and a coefficients table with Gelman-standardized coefficients and odds ratios (Exp(b)).

Usage

jlogistic(
  formula,
  data,
  subset = NULL,
  variable.id = NULL,
  numeric = NULL,
  categorical = NULL,
  count = NULL,
  ci = NULL,
  classification = FALSE,
  diagnostics = NULL,
  ref.categories = NULL,
  full = FALSE,
  case.processing.detail = NULL,
  digits = NULL,
  ...,
  value.id = NULL,
  model.layout = NULL,
  std = "gelman"
)

Arguments

formula

A model formula, e.g. DV ~ IV1 + IV2. The DV must be a binary variable coded 0/1, and a variable of the data: a computed term on the left, such as I(Score > 50), is refused, so create the 0/1 variable first. Transformed predictor terms such as log(IV1) are computed automatically and used throughout the output.

data

A data frame containing variables referenced in formula.

subset

An optional unquoted logical expression (e.g. Group == 1) to subset cases for this call only. Written in R syntax and checked the way jsubset() checks a filter: subset = NOT(Age < 40), for example, is refused with the corrected subset = !(Age < 40) shown (see jsubset for a translation table).

variable.id

Character or NULL. Variable label display mode: one of "both", "names", "labels", "legend", or "legend.bottom". "names" shows variable names only; "both" shows "name: label"; "labels" replaces each coefficient's variable name with its label in the Coefficients table (factor level decoration is preserved) – best for short labels; "legend" prints a label legend just below the Coefficients table (at the coefficients/fit seam); "legend.bottom" prints it at the very end. NULL (default) defers to joutput()'s variable.id setting. Not a logical.

numeric

Optional. Variables to treat as continuous even if they have value labels, named bare or in quotes, several with c().

categorical

Optional. Variables to treat as categorical even if they lack value labels, named bare or in quotes, several with c(): categorical = Region.

count

Optional. Independent variables to treat as counts for this call (the per-call counterpart of jcount()), named bare or in quotes, several with c(). A count predictor is numeric-like, so it enters the model exactly as numeric would; the argument is provided for symmetry with the other analysis functions. The binary dependent variable is fixed, so naming it here has no effect. A variable cannot be listed in both count and categorical.

ci

Logical or NULL. If TRUE, adds 95% confidence intervals for Exp(b). If NULL (default), defers to joutput().

classification

Logical. If TRUE, prints a classification table showing predicted vs observed outcomes. Default is FALSE.

diagnostics

Logical, character vector, or NULL. If TRUE, prints the VIF table (for a model with two or more predictors) and draws three diagnostic plots: binned residuals, Cook's distance, and residuals against leverage. A character vector names the ones to show: vif, binned, cooks, leverage, more than one combined with c(), as in diagnostics = c("vif", "cooks"); a name that is not one of these is an error. The VIF values are the predictors' ordinary variance inflation factors, computed from their correlations as for a linear model. A VIF above 10 gets a line of interpretation under the table, except at joutput("minimal"). In a model with a predictor of three or more categories the table gives each predictor one row with its generalized VIF, Df and GVIF^(1/(2*Df)), the dummy variables sharing a row, as in jlm(); computed from the correlations, these differ a little from car::vif() on a glm, which uses the coefficients' covariance. If NULL (default), defers to joutput()'s diagnostics setting, which is off at every output level until it is set. The plots, and the probability, ROC, calibration and odds-ratio plots, are available afterwards from jplot() on the returned object.

ref.categories

Logical or NULL. Per-call override for showing the reference-categories block (the baseline level dropped from each set of dummy variables). NULL (default) defers to joutput()'s ref.categories setting. Applies to jlm() and jlogistic() only, since they are the functions that produce dummy-coded coefficient tables.

full

Logical. If TRUE, turns on ci and classification. Does not override an explicit FALSE, and does not turn on diagnostics, which diagnostics alone governs.

case.processing.detail

Per-call override of the Case Processing Summary detail tier: one of "none", "totals", or "per_code". NULL (default) uses the active joutput() level default. The Case Processing table itself prints only when a filter or listwise deletion excluded cases; otherwise a one-line N statement takes its place. See ?joutput (case.processing).

digits

Integer or NULL. Number of decimal places for continuous statistics in the output tables (range 0-7; digits = 0 prints whole numbers with no trailing decimal point). Does not affect p-values, percentages, or integer quantities (counts, N, degrees of freedom), which keep their own fixed conventions. NULL (default) defers to joutput()'s digits setting (default 3).

...

Reserved for argument-name checking. Passing which, plots, or show will produce a helpful error suggesting diagnostics instead.

value.id

Character or NULL. Value-label display mode for the dummy category rows in the Coefficients table: one of "both" ("code: label", degrading to a bare code where a code has no label), "values" (the bare code), or "labels" (the value label, degrading to the bare code where none exists). The reference category folded into each grouped variable's header follows the same mode. "legend" and "legend.bottom" are not supported here: a coefficient table already pairs each value label with its row, so a separate legend block would only duplicate it. Passing either explicitly is an error; a joutput() default of "legend" or "legend.bottom" is tolerated and rendered as "both", so it does not break a bare call. Variables with no value labels render identically under all supported modes. NULL (default) defers to joutput()'s value.id setting. Applies only to multi-category dummy predictors; continuous and single-contrast (dichotomous) predictors are unaffected. Not a logical.

model.layout

Character or NULL. The order of the coefficient table and the fit statistics: "coefficients" (the default) prints the Coefficients table first and the fit block after it; "fit" prints the fit block first, for readers who look at the model as a whole before its coefficients. The Case Processing block, the diagnostics and the other tables stay where they are. NULL (default) defers to joutput()'s model.layout setting.

std

Character. The standardized-coefficient column, between p and Exp(b). One of "gelman" (default) – Gelman (2008) scaling, headed "Gelman beta"; "product" – each column of the model scaled as it stands, the product of an interaction and a squared term included (headed "Product beta"); or "none" – omit the column. See the section Standardized coefficients. jlm()'s regular standardization ("regular", "all") divides by the outcome's standard deviation, which a binary outcome does not have, and is not available here. The returned object carries both columns' full values (beta_gelman, beta_product) whichever is shown.

Value

Invisibly returns a list of class jst_logistic containing:

model

The fitted glm object.

model_type

Character string logistic.

model_frame

The model frame used to fit the model.

formula_used

The formula after dummy expansion.

coefficients

Formatted coefficient table (data frame).

coefficients_raw

Flat data frame of raw, full-precision coefficient statistics (one row per coefficient): term (machine key, shared with jlm), b, SE, Wald, df, p, exp_b, exp_ci_lower / exp_ci_upper odds-ratio CI bounds (present regardless of the ci display toggle), beta_gelman and beta_product (the full standardized coefficients, whichever std shows). Carries beta_standardization and outcome attributes.

fit_raw

List of raw, full-precision model-level fit statistics: ll_model, ll_null, deviance, null_deviance, the omnibus likelihood-ratio test (chi_sq, omnibus_df, omnibus_p), Cox & Snell and Nagelkerke pseudo R-squared (cox_snell_r2, nagelkerke_r2), aic, and n.

nagelkerke_r2

Nagelkerke pseudo R-squared.

cox_snell_r2

Cox & Snell pseudo R-squared.

neg2ll

-2 Log Likelihood.

aic

Akaike Information Criterion.

omnibus

Named vector: chi_square, df, p.

n

Number of observations.

predicts

Character string describing what the model predicts.

dummy_coef_names

Names of dummy variable columns.

ref_cats

Reference category descriptions.

dummy_groups

Named list, one element per dummy-coded variable: labels, its categories as the coefficient table labels them, and dummy, the dummy column of each (NA for the reference). Used by jplot().

vif

Named numeric vector of VIF values, or NULL.

gvif

The generalized VIFs, when the model has a set of dummy variables (a predictor of three or more categories): a data frame of term, GVIF, Df and GVIF_adj (GVIF^(1/(2*Df))), one row per predictor, as the VIF table prints them; NULL otherwise.

sample_info

Pipeline and missing data counts.

Details

The dependent variable must be coded 0/1. If it is not, the function stops with a clear error message and suggests the appropriate jrecode() command.

Handles haven-labelled variables, registered dummy variables via jdummy(), and the numeric/categorical overrides in the same way as jlm().

A predictor dropped because it is an exact linear combination of the others is named in a warning, as in jlm(). A model with no predictors, y ~ 1, is fitted too: its one coefficient is the log odds of the modeled category, the pseudo R-squared values are 0, and the Omnibus Test, which compares the model with that one, reads "None: the model has no predictors to test." (its p is NA in the returned object).

Transformed predictor terms in formula are computed automatically. A term that applies a function to a variable – log(x), sqrt(x), exp(x), I(x^2), scale(x), an arithmetic expression, or a logical condition such as I(x > 10) – is evaluated once on the analysis data and enters the model as a single derived column named for the expression, so the coefficient table and the diagnostics report the term as written. This follows the base R formula convention; the terms supported inline are those that evaluate to one numeric or logical column. Terms that produce several columns (poly(x, 2), spline bases) or a categorical result (cut(x, 3)) are not supported inline: create the derived variable as a column of the data first, then name that column in the formula. (The dependent variable must be a plain 0/1 dichotomy, so a transform applies to predictors, not the response.) A categorical variable may be compared but not transformed. I(x == 2), I(x %in% c(1, 3)) and, for a text variable, I(x == "web") each enter the model as a TRUE/FALSE predictor, as in lm(); an order comparison such as I(x >= 3) does too when x holds numbers. Arithmetic on a categorical x – log(x), I(x^2) – is refused, because it would be computed from the category codes; register x with jnumeric if its codes are meant as numbers. A value or vector from your workspace may be named inside a computed term, as in lm(): I(x > cutoff) with cutoff <- 10. A data frame may not: write y ~ x with data = MyData, not MyData$y ~ MyData$x. A variable may not: jstats analyzes the variables of a data frame, so a vector holding one value for each case – w in I(x * w), or an object reached with $ such as lst$w – is added to the data frame first (MyData$w <- w), where lm() would read it from the workspace; the stop gives that line. A vector of any other length used value by value is refused, where lm() would repeat the shorter one; a set used with %in% may have any length.

In a formula, ^ applied to a single variable is not arithmetic: it is R's operator for interactions up to that order, so x^2 enters the model as x alone. Write I(x^2) for the square. jlogistic() fits the model as written and then warns when a formula does this. A power that is not a number, x^k, stops with an error, as in lm(); write I(x^k).

Interactions

An interaction is entered in the formula with *, as in R: y ~ x * z fits x, z and their product, and the product's row in the coefficient table is labeled x * z. With a categorical predictor registered with jdummy, the interaction rows are grouped under a header naming the reference category, with one row per dummy variable, as the predictor's own rows are. Each row's b is the change in the log-odds slope of one variable per unit of the other (or, for a dummy row, the difference in slope between that category and the reference), and its Exp(b) the factor by which the other variable's odds ratio is multiplied per unit; the main-effect rows give the slopes where the other variable is zero. jplot on the result draws the probability plots.

Standardized coefficients

A logistic regression's coefficients are in each predictor's own units, so they cannot be compared across predictors measured differently. The Gelman beta column puts them on one footing (Gelman, 2008): the model is refit with every predictor centered, a continuous predictor also divided by two standard deviations and a binary predictor (a 0/1 variable, or a category's dummy variable) left on its one-unit scale. A continuous predictor's Gelman beta is then the change in the log-odds for a move from one standard deviation below its mean to one above, and a binary predictor's the difference between its two groups, so the two are comparable; exp() of a Gelman beta is the odds ratio for that move. The outcome is not standardized – it has no standard deviation to standardize by, which is why fully standardized logistic coefficients are contested and this column uses Gelman's scaling. It is the column jlm(std = "gelman") gives a linear model, computed the same way.

A computed term that is a power or a product of variables, such as I(x^2) or I(x * z), is recomputed from the rescaled variables (Gelman, 2008, section 3.1), as an interaction written x * z is. In a model with an interaction or a squared term the predictors are centered, so a main effect's Gelman beta is its effect at the average of the variable it interacts with, while its b is the effect where that variable is 0; the two can differ in sign, and a note under the table says so. A variable that equals the product of two other predictors, or the square of one, is named in a note of its own, since the column treats it as an ordinary predictor.

std = "product" instead scales each column of the model as it stands – b times two standard deviations of the column, a binary column's b unchanged – the product of an interaction and a squared term included, the convention of software that computes a product as a new variable. On a model without such terms the two columns agree.

References

Gelman, A. (2008). Scaling regression inputs by dividing by two standard deviations. Statistics in Medicine, 27(15), 2865-2873.

See also

jstats for the package overview, workflow conventions, and complete function listing.

Examples

# With explicit data frame -- Volunteer is already coded 0/1
jlogistic(Volunteer ~ Income + Age, data = community)
#> Logistic Regression
#> 
#> Case Processing    Excluded  Remaining

#>     Auto-listwise         6         97
#>     Analysis N           --         97
#> 
#> Missing data   From 103   %
#>     Income
#>       Missing      6     5.8
#> --------------------------------------
#> 
#> Coefficients
#>                 b      SE    Wald   df    p    Gelman β  Exp(b)
#> -----------  ------  -----  ------  --  -----  --------  ------

#> Income        0.000  0.000   6.683   1   .010    1.266    1.000

#> 
#> Outcome: Volunteer

#> Chi-Square  df    p
